text: The reception history of the *bnei elohim*, the "sons of God" in Genesis 6, is one of the stranger chapters in biblical interpretation. The Book of Enoch, an ancient Jewish work preserved most fully in Ethiopic versions and received as scripture by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, expands the passage into an account of fallen angels: the Watchers descend, corrupt humanity through forbidden teaching, and corrupt humanity through miscegenation. Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 may assume this angelic reading. Augustine, in *City of God*, rejected it and preferred the Sethite interpretation, in which the "sons of God" are the godly line of Seth and the daughters of men belong to the line of Cain. Other readers have compared Genesis 6 with ancient Near Eastern traditions in which kings and other powerful men claimed descent from gods. The flood narrative introduced there also belongs to a wider Mesopotamian flood tradition, preserved most fully in the *Atrahasis* epic and in tablet XI of the *Epic of Gilgamesh*, the Utnapishtim narrative, where close parallels to the biblical flood story appear. The Hebrew word for Noah’s vessel is *tevah* ("ark," "chest"), used elsewhere in Scripture only for the basket in which the infant Moses is set adrift on the Nile.
